claims.text: Adding approximately 5 at% Al to a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy will promote ordered intermetallic precipitate formation.
The Al-induced precipitates may be gamma-TiAl-like phases.
The ordered precipitates will hinder dislocation motion.
Hindering dislocation motion through Al-induced precipitation will improve elevated-temperature mechanical properties relative to the alloy without Al.
The initial material contains titanium and nickel as primary constituents plus at least three additional elements, each at roughly 5–35 at%.
The initial alloy is produced by conventional melting and casting.
The intervention is the introduction of approximately 5 at% Al during alloy processing.
The relevant elevated-temperature test range is 600–800°C.
A finely dispersed population of ordered intermetallic precipitates will form within the disordered high-entropy matrix.
Al promotes the nucleation and growth of ordered intermetallic precipitates in this alloy.
The precipitates act as obstacles to dislocation motion and produce precipitation strengthening at elevated temperature.
The Al-added alloy will have significantly greater high-temperature tensile strength than an otherwise identical alloy without Al.
The Al-added alloy will have significantly greater high-temperature creep resistance than an otherwise identical alloy without Al.
Direct evidence for the effect of Al in titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloys is lacking.
The precipitate volume fraction and optimal Al content are uncertain.
